recipe.history:
Feta is one of the oldest cheeses in recorded human history, with roots stretching back over 8,000 years to the mountainous terrain of Greece. The word itself derives from the Italian 'fetta,' meaning slice, but the cheese is thoroughly, unapologetically Greek — so much so that the European Union granted it Protected Designation of Origin status in 2002, meaning that only cheese produced in specific regions of Greece from local sheep's milk (or a blend with up to 30% goat's milk) may legally bear the name. Crumbled into salads, baked into spanakopita, drizzled with olive oil and scattered with oregano, feta carries the salt of the Aegean in every bite. Its sharp, tangy, slightly briny flavor profile is the direct result of the animals grazing on the wild herbs and grasses of the Greek hillsides — a terroir as distinct and storied as any wine.

Feta's arrival in American cuisine was, like so many culinary migrations, carried on the backs of immigrants. Greek communities settling in cities like Chicago, New York, and Baltimore in the early twentieth century brought their pantry staples with them, and feta — packed in brine, hardy enough to travel — made the crossing. For decades it remained an insider ingredient, beloved within Greek-American households and diasporic restaurants but largely unknown to the broader public. That changed gradually through the latter half of the century as American palates grew more adventurous. By the 1990s and 2000s, feta had escaped the Greek salad and began appearing on flatbreads, in omelets, and — inevitably, gloriously — on burgers. The fat content of feta, lower than cheddar but intensely flavorful, means a little goes a long way. On a burger it doesn't melt so much as soften and warm, clinging to the patty and releasing its saltiness in bursts rather than as a uniform blanket. It was only a matter of time before some inspired short-order cook decided that a beef patty needed the company of Greece's most famous export.

I remember the first time I put feta on a burger — not in a restaurant, but standing over a cast-iron skillet in a cramped apartment kitchen, the windows fogged with steam, the radio playing something I've since forgotten. I'd had leftover feta from a salad the night before, sitting in its little plastic tub of brine in the back of the fridge, and I thought: why not? What followed was one of those accidental kitchen revelations that you spend the rest of your life trying to reproduce with intention. The saltiness cut through the richness of the beef. The slight chalkiness of the cheese gave the bite a texture I hadn't expected — something between a crumble and a cream. There was something almost Mediterranean about it, like the burger had been on a long vacation somewhere sunny and come back a more interesting version of itself. Every time I make this burger now, I'm back in that kitchen, slightly amazed that two such different things could belong so completely together.

Cooking a burger to medium rare is not a preference — it is a conviction. At an internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the proteins in the beef have tightened just enough to give the patty structure and a proper crust on the outside, while the interior remains a deep, rosy pink, soft, yielding, and swimming in its own rendered fat and juices. This is the temperature at which beef tastes most like itself. Cook it further and you are not making a better burger — you are making a different, diminished thing. The juices that would have pooled at the center are driven out, the fat has rendered past the point of richness into dryness, and what remains is gray and apologetic. With feta in particular, medium rare matters even more: the warm, barely-set interior of the patty provides a contrast to the cool, briny crumble of the cheese that you simply cannot achieve if the meat is overcooked and desiccated. To serve this burger well-done is to misunderstand what it is trying to be. Medium rare is not a temperature — it is an argument for paying attention.
ingredients: 300g bread flour, plus extra for dusting
3 large eggs, at room temperature (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
700g freshly ground beef — 80% lean chuck, 20% fat (ground to order or ground at home for best results)
1 tablespoon neutral oil (such as canola or grapeseed) for cooking
200g full-fat Greek feta cheese (packed in brine), drained and patted dry
60g full-fat cream cheese, at room temperature
2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, plus extra for drizzling
1 teaspoon fresh thyme leaves (or 1/4 teaspoon dried)
1 tablespoon fresh oregano leaves, finely chopped
1 teaspoon fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
2 cups baby arugula, washed and dried
1 medium English cucumber, thinly sliced into rounds
1 medium ripe tomato, sliced into thick rounds
1/2 small red onion, thinly sliced into rings
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUN DOUGH: In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with a dough hook, combine the bread flour, instant yeast, sugar, and salt. Whisk briefly to combine. Add 2 eggs and the warm milk. Mix on low speed until a shaggy dough forms, about 2 minutes. Increase to medium speed and knead for 5 minutes until the dough comes together and pulls away from the sides of the bowl.

2. ADD THE BUTTER: With the mixer running on medium-low, add the softened butter one cube at a time, waiting until each piece is fully incorporated before adding the next. This process will take 8 to 10 minutes. The dough will look messy and almost broken at points — keep going. Once all butter is incorporated, increase speed to medium-high and knead for another 5 minutes until the dough is smooth, glossy, and slightly tacky but not sticky. It should pass the windowpane test (stretch a small piece thin enough to see light through without tearing).

3. FIRST RISE: Shape the dough into a ball, place in a lightly oiled bowl, and cover tightly with plastic wrap. Let rise at room temperature until doubled in size, approximately 1.5 to 2 hours. Alternatively, refrigerate overnight for a slow rise and richer flavor — remove from the fridge 1 hour before shaping.

4. SHAPE THE BUNS: Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 135g each). Working one piece at a time, fold the edges of the dough underneath itself to create surface tension, then cup your hand over the dough and roll it against the work surface in tight circles until you have a smooth, taut ball. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing at least 3 inches apart. Flatten each ball gently with your palm to roughly 3.5 inches in diameter.
5. SECOND RISE: Cover the buns loosely with lightly oiled plastic wrap and let rise at room temperature until puffy and roughly doubled, about 1 to 1.5 hours.

6. BAKE THE BUNS: Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Beat the remaining egg with 1 tablespoon of water to make an egg wash. Brush each bun gently with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds if using. Bake for 16 to 18 minutes, rotating the pan halfway through, until deep golden brown. The internal temperature of the buns should read 190°F (88°C). Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing.

7. MAKE THE WHIPPED FETA SPREAD: Combine the drained feta, cream cheese, olive oil, lemon juice, minced garlic, black pepper, and thyme in a food processor. Process for 2 to 3 minutes, stopping to scrape down the sides as needed, until the mixture is completely smooth, light, and spreadable. Taste and adjust lemon juice or pepper as needed. Transfer to a bowl, cover, and refrigerate until ready to use. (Can be made up to 3 days ahead.)
8. MAKE THE HERB OIL: In a small bowl, whisk together the olive oil, chopped oregano, parsley, and lemon zest. Set aside at room temperature to let the flavors meld.

9. FORM THE PATTIES: Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions (approximately 175g each). Handle the meat as little as possible — overworking it will result in a dense, tough patty. Gently form each portion into a loose ball, then flatten into a disk about 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Use your thumb to press a shallow dimple into the center of each patty — this prevents the burger from puffing up into a dome as it cooks. Season both sides generously with kosher salt and black pepper immediately before cooking.

10. COOK THE PATTIES TO MEDIUM RARE: Heat a cast-iron skillet or heavy-bottomed pan over high heat until it is smoking hot, approximately 3 to 4 minutes. Add the neutral oil and swirl to coat. Place the patties in the pan, pressing down gently with a spatula for the first 10 seconds to ensure full contact with the surface. Cook undisturbed for 3 minutes until a deep mahogany crust forms on the bottom. Flip once and cook for an additional 2 to 2.5 minutes. Use an instant-read thermometer to check the internal temperature — you are aiming for 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. The center will be a deep, rosy pink. Remove the patties from the pan and let them rest on a wire rack for 3 to 5 minutes. Do not tent with foil — this creates steam and softens the crust.

11. TOAST THE BUNS: While the patties rest, slice each brioche bun in half horizontally. Melt 1 tablespoon of butter in the same pan used for the patties (do not wipe it out — those fond drippings are flavor). Place the buns cut-side down and toast over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes until golden and lightly crisped. Watch carefully — brioche browns quickly.

12. ASSEMBLE THE BURGER: Spread a generous tablespoon of whipped feta on the cut face of the bottom bun. Lay down a few cucumber slices, followed by a slice of tomato and a small handful of arugula. Place the rested patty directly on top of the arugula. Scatter 15g of crumbled feta over the hot patty. Drizzle 1 teaspoon of herb oil over the feta and patty. Finish with a few rings of red onion and a pinch of flaky sea salt. Spread a thin layer of whipped feta on the cut face of the top bun and set it in place.

13. SERVE IMMEDIATELY: The Foot Feta-ish Burger must be served at once, while the patty is still resting-warm, the feta crumbles are just beginning to soften against the meat, and the brioche bun retains its toasted crunch. Cut in half on the diagonal if desired for presentation. Serve with nothing that would compete — this burger is the thing.
